problem.statement: WPF developers lack a reliable way to determine whether binding UI elements to struct properties (which WPF boxes on each access) creates strong references that leak memory over time.

persona.primary: WPF/.NET developer maintaining legacy desktop applications

context.situation: A developer binding a UI element to a nested property of an immutable struct on an INotifyPropertyChanged class is unsure whether WPF's struct-boxing behavior causes a memory leak.

current_workarounds: Binding directly to the struct property itself (e.g. {Binding Demo}) instead of a nested property (e.g. {Binding Demo.Value}) to avoid WPF attaching event handlers

possible_wedges.offer: A memory-leak analyzer/profiler for legacy WPF apps that flags binding expressions likely to leak via struct boxing.
A static-analysis CLI that scans XAML/code-behind for struct-typed binding paths and reports leak risk with suggested fixes.
A Visual Studio/Roslyn analyzer extension that warns inline when a XAML binding targets a nested struct property.

risks: Single evidence item (one Stack Overflow-style question) - no corroborating reports of actual leaks or business impact
No named competing tools or products in the evidence, so market awareness/demand is unverified
Unclear willingness to pay - question shows technical curiosity, not commercial intent or urgency (low pain/urgency/commercial_intent signals)
Question may be adequately answered by community discussion alone, reducing need for a dedicated tool
Narrow niche: only applies to WPF apps binding to struct properties on INotifyPropertyChanged classes

cheapest_experiment.hypothesis: WPF developers maintaining legacy apps would try a free lightweight checker that flags XAML bindings to struct properties as potential leak risks.
cheapest_experiment.input: A short blog post or forum reply (SO, r/csharp, WPF Discord) answering the struct-boxing leak question, offering a free script/checklist in exchange for email signup.
cheapest_experiment.output: Number of email signups or tool downloads from the post over 2 weeks.
cheapest_experiment.commitment_event: Developer submits email to receive the checker script or clicks through to download it.
cheapest_experiment.success_threshold: 15+ signups/downloads from a single post, or unsolicited follow-up questions asking for a deeper tool.
cheapest_experiment.failure_threshold: Fewer than 5 signups/downloads despite reasonable post visibility (upvotes/views).
